title: Chapter 68: A Thing Put Back, Part 1 of 5: Reading in the Dark
html:
Juno read under the blanket, because that was where you read when you were not supposed to be reading.
Nobody had told her she was not supposed to. Her mother would not have minded. Her mother would have been pleased, in her tired quiet way, and said, well, look at you, and gone back to her mending. But it felt like a thing you did in secret. Like eating a stolen bun. So Juno did it in secret, at night, under the blanket, with the candle stub in the tin lid propped on her knees and the blanket made into a tent over her head and the book open on her lap.
It was very hot in the tent and very cold everywhere else. Her nose ran. Her feet, at the bottom of the bed, outside the tent, were two lumps of ice, and they ached, the way they always ached now, deep inside, in the bones, since the night she had walked fourteen miles to the barge with the snow coming in through her boots. Doctor Silas said they would always ache a bit, in the cold. He said she was lucky to have kept her toes. Gideon had not kept all of his.
She did not think about her feet. She thought about the letters.
The book was called HARBOUR TIDE TABLES. That was what it said on the front, in old gold letters, rubbed off at the corners. She could read that now. She had worked it out three nights ago, letter by letter, sounding each one with her lips. H. A. R. B. It had taken her most of an hour. And then she had felt like a fool, because it did not mean anything. It was not about tides at all. Inside, there were no tides. Inside there was only the harvester.
His writing.
It went on page after page after page. Big letters, all capitals, leaning hard to the right, as if they were walking uphill into a wind. Some of them too big. Some of them wobbly. All of them in pencil, gone soft and gray and smudgy where the pages had rubbed together. It was hard. It was harder than anything she had ever done, harder than carrying a message across the city in the dark, harder than walking on frozen feet. Every word was a wall. You had to climb it, one letter at a time, and at the top there was the next one.
But she was climbing.
She could do the letters now. All of them. A to Z. Lyra had taught her, before she went. Lyra could not write anymore, but she could read, and she could point. She had sat with Juno in the crypt with the book open and pointed at each letter with her gloved finger and said it, and Juno had said it back, over and over, until her head swam. And then Lyra had gone north with the harvester and the big captain in the snow, and Juno had been left with a book she could not read, under her mattress, and the letters going round and round in her head.
So she read. A little every night. Under the blanket.
She was a long way in now. She had read the first page. That one was easy, because Lyra had read it out loud to Corin in the crypt and Juno had heard her, and she remembered some of the words, so when she came to them on the page she knew them. YOUR NAME IS CORIN VANE. That was the first line. She knew that one by heart. She had traced it with her finger so many times that the pencil had gone shiny.
Then pages about people. Names, mostly, and then things about them. She did not understand most of it. Some of it was about the Ministry and things the harvester had done there, and the words were long, and she skipped them. Some of it was about Lyra. A lot of it was about Lyra. Juno did not read those pages very hard. They felt private. Like listening at a door.
And tonight she had come to a page with a heading on it.
It was in bigger letters than the rest. Underlined twice. She had stopped and looked at it for a long time before she started, because big letters at the top of a page meant something important, and she wanted to get it right.
THOSE I OWE.
It took her a while. THOSE was hard, because the O and the S and the E did not sound like themselves. OWE was worse. She sounded it out four times. Oh. Wuh. Eh. Owe. Then she understood it, all at once, and sat back under the blanket with the candle flame shaking.
Those I owe.
And under it, a list.
Names. One under the other. Some of them she knew. Some she did not. Some had a line through them. Some had a little drawing beside them, a flower, or a cross. She went down them slowly, with her finger, sounding each one with her lips.
NED. She knew Ned. Bet's brother. Ned who forgot how to swallow, in the crypt, before the sixth bell. He had a line through him.
GIDEON. And next to it, smaller, H.291 TO 340. She did not know what that meant.
BIG GIDEON. SAUL.
Saul had a line through him too.
SILAS.
MRS DOYLE.
WAT.
And then, near the bottom of the page, in letters that were a little smaller and a little more careful than the rest, as if he had taken trouble over them:
JUNO. SHE WALKED FOURTEEN MILES ON FROZEN FEET. SHE CARRIED THE LETTER.
Juno stopped.
She sat in the hot little tent of the blanket with the candle shaking in the tin lid and her finger on the page, and read it again. Slowly. Every letter. To make sure.
J. U. N. O.
It was her. It was her name. In his writing. In his book.
She did not know why her eyes were stinging. It was the smoke from the candle, probably. Tallow candles always smoked.
She read the rest of it. Slowly. SHE WALKED FOURTEEN MILES. She knew FOURTEEN, because it was a number and numbers had been in the book before. She knew MILES because Lyra had said it. She sounded out FROZEN. She sounded out FEET. SHE CARRIED THE LETTER.
He owed her.
The harvester, with the gray hands, who was on every wall in the city now on a poster, who had held the roof up on Midwinter night, or so everybody said. He had written her name in his book under a heading that said THOSE I OWE.
Juno sat very still for a long time.
Then she licked her thumb and finger and pinched out the candle, very carefully, so as not to waste it, and lay down in the dark with the book under her pillow instead of under the mattress, and her hand flat on top of it, and did not sleep for a long time.
Mrs. Marta's Room
The clocks woke her. They always did.
Not because they struck. They did not strike. None of them did, not one, out of the forty-one clocks in her mother's room. They ticked. That was all. Forty-one clocks on the walls and the shelves and the mantel and the top of the dresser and the floor in the corners, all ticking, all at once, all slightly out of time with each other, so that the room was full of a soft endless dry pattering like rain on a roof. And none of them was right. None of them had been set. Some said three o'clock and some said nine and one, a little black one with a painted bird on it, said a quarter to midnight and had said it as long as Juno could remember.
They had been her father's. He had mended them. People brought him clocks that would not go, and he made them go, and then the people did not come back for them, or could not pay, and so the clocks stayed. On every wall. Going. He used to say that a clock that went was a clock that was happy, and it did not matter what time it said, so long as it went.
He had been gone four years. The clocks still went. Her mother wound them every Sunday, every one, with a key on a string, and never set a single one.
Juno lay in the dark under the blanket and listened to them, and knew from the feel of the cold that it was not yet morning.
The room was small. It was the whole of where they lived, her and her mother. One room, at the back of number fourteen, at street level, through a purple door at the end of a passage that smelled of coal and cats. There was the range against one wall, black iron, with the fire banked down in it for the night under a shovel of ash, and the kettle on the side. There was the table in the middle, scrubbed white, with two chairs. There was the dresser with the plates on it, and the clocks on the plates. There was her mother's bed, in the corner by the range where it was warmest, with the curtain pulled round it. And there was Juno's bed, which was a straw mattress on a low wooden frame in the other corner, by the window, where it was coldest, because Juno had said she did not mind the cold, which was a lie.
The window had frost on it. On the inside. Thick white ferns of it, all over the glass, so that the gray light from the yard outside came through it soft and blurred.
On the shelf above the range, between a clock with a brass face and a clock with no face at all, there was a tin. A tea tin, red, with a picture of a ship on it, the paint mostly rubbed off. The rent tin. Every Friday her mother put money in it, and every Monday the landlord's man came and took it out. Juno knew, without looking, how much was in it this morning. Not enough. There had not been enough for three weeks. Her mother had not said so. Her mother never said so. But Juno had seen her, last night, take the tin down and open it and look inside and put it back without putting anything in, and stand for a long moment with her hand on the shelf.
The cold came up through the straw mattress.
Juno lay there and listened to the clocks, and to her mother's breathing behind the curtain, slow and even and tired, and thought about the book under her pillow. About her name in it. SHE WALKED FOURTEEN MILES ON FROZEN FEET.
She had walked it. She did not remember most of it. She remembered the snow, and the cold, and the bridges, twenty-three of them, which she had counted because Lyra would have counted them. She remembered the locks. She remembered her feet stopping hurting, which was the worst part, because Doctor Silas said afterward that was when you should start being frightened. She remembered Hessa's barge in the dark, and Wat's big hands lifting her down. And she remembered the letter, the whole way, in the pocket of her coat, against her chest, folded in three. Lyra's letter to her brother. The one she had carried all the way out to the barge and all the way back again, and then given to a tall cadet with Lyra's eyes at the pump in Gallows Lane.
She had done that. That was a true thing. It was in the book.
She turned over on the mattress, careful of her feet, and looked at the clocks.
The little black one with the painted bird on it said a quarter to midnight.
And from the passage outside the purple door, very softly, there came a scratching.
Juno went still.
It was not the cats. The cats scratched low down, at the bottom of the door, and mewed. This was higher. At the height of a hand. Fingernails, on wood. Three scratches, quick. A pause. Then two more, slower.
She knew that knock. Not that exact one. But that kind. She had used it herself, a dozen times this winter, at a dozen doors in the dark. It was the knock you used when you did not want to wake the house. When you did not want anyone to hear you but the one person you had come for.
Behind the curtain, her mother's breathing did not change. She was asleep. She slept hard, these days.
Juno got out of bed.
She did it without a sound, the way she had learned on the rooftops, rolling off the mattress onto the cold boards and getting her feet under her slowly. Her feet hurt. She ignored them. She pulled her coat on over her shift and buttoned it to the chin, and pushed her bare feet into her boots without lacing them, and went across the room between the ticking clocks to the purple door.
She did not open it.
She put her mouth to the crack at the edge of it, where the wood did not meet the frame, and whispered.
"Who is it?"
A pause. Then a voice, on the other side. A man's voice. Very low and very fast and very frightened, the words tumbling over each other like apples out of a sack.
"Is this Mrs. Marta's? Number fourteen, the back, the purple door? Only I've been to three doors already and one of them had a dog, and I don't like dogs, and I need a girl called Juno, she's quick and she talks fast, he said, and if you're her then I've got something for you, and if you're not then I'm very sorry to have woken you, and I'll go away."
Juno stared at the door.
Then she lifted the latch.
A Scratch at the Door
The man in the passage was gray.
Not gray like the harvester's hands. Gray like a road. Gray all over, with dust and mud and cold and tiredness, from his boots to the red woolen cap pulled down over his ears. The cap was the only color on him, and even that had gone brownish with dirt. His long coat was gray with dried mud to the knees. His face, between the cap and a red scarf pulled down under his chin, was thin and freckled and very young and so tired that the skin round his eyes had gone the color of a bruise.
He was holding a stub of candle in a tin dish, and the flame shook.
"You're her," he said. "You're Juno. You've got to be. He said you talk fast, and you've got a look about you like you talk fast."
"Who said?"
"Him." The man looked over his shoulder, up the dark passage toward the street door, the way a bird looks round. "Him with the gray hands. The harvester. Up north."
Juno's heart went over.
"You've seen him?"
"Four days ago. Up at the end of the world. In a camp full of people with lines painted on their faces who I was sure were going to eat me and didn't." He looked back at her. "He gave me a thing. For a boy. Called Gideon. At a church with a crypt, twenty-three steps down. And if not the boy, then you." He swallowed. "I went to the church first. Last night. Late. Only there were men in the lane. Gray coats. Standing about by the steps, smoking, like they were waiting for something. So I didn't go down. I came here."
He put his free hand inside his coat. Deep, on the left side, against his chest. And brought out a packet.
It was small. Flat. Wrapped in a square of some dark stiff cloth, oily and shiny, the kind sailors use to keep things dry. Tied round with a leather thong. The cloth was creased and warm from being against his chest for four days. It smelled, very faintly, of bread, and smoke, and something sweet and dark that Juno did not know.
He held it out.
She took it.
It was very light. Lighter than she had expected. Just a piece of paper inside the cloth, she thought. One piece. Folded. She could feel the edges of it through the oilcloth.
"Quick," said the man.
Juno looked up.
"That's what he said to tell you. If I forgot everything else." The man's face screwed up with the effort of remembering. "Quick, he said, and warm. Quick and warm." He shook his head. "I don't know what it means and I don't want to."
"Quick and warm," said Juno.
"Quick and warm." He was already backing away from her up the passage, with the candle shaking. "And he said read it slow. To you. Read it slow. He wrote that on it, I think. At the bottom. I watched him. He wrote very slow, like he was making every letter out of wood."
"Wait," said Juno. "Wait. Is he all right? Is she? Lyra? And the captain?"
The man stopped.
He stood in the dark passage with his candle and looked at her, and for a moment his thin frightened freckled face went still, as if he were trying to decide how much was true.
"They were alive," he said. "Four days ago. On the edge. The lady was cross and the captain was sharpening his sword and the harvester was humming." He paused. "Humming like an old man. I don't know why." Another pause, and his eyes went over his shoulder again. "And there were carts on the north road. Closed ones. Going up after them. With something in them that ticked."
Juno did not say anything.
"That's all I know," said the man. "That's all. I'm going home now. I'm going to lock my door and get drunk and not come out till spring."
And he turned and went away up the passage, fast, with the candle going out in the draft before he reached the street door, so that the last she saw of him was a thin dark shape in a red cap against the gray of the street, and then nothing.
The street door banged.
Juno stood in the doorway of her mother's room with the oilcloth packet in her hand and the forty-one clocks ticking behind her.
Then she shut the purple door, very quietly, and went back across the room to the table, and sat down, and put the packet on the scrubbed white boards in front of her.
She did not open it.
The gray light through the frost on the window was getting stronger. The room was coming out of the dark. The black range. The dresser. The clocks. The rent tin on the shelf with the ship on it.
She looked at the packet.
Quick and warm. Read it slow.
She did not know what it was. But she knew who it was for. She had sat in the crypt of Saint Bride's with Gideon a dozen times in the last week, on the bottom step, while he whittled his little boats with a knife too big for his hand and did not talk. She knew what he was waiting for. Everybody in the crypt knew. Lord Thorne had not been dead a day before Gideon had gone to Doctor Silas with Linus's book under his arm and said, flat, the way he said everything, "It says how to put a thing back. If you're quick. It doesn't say how. He said he'd send it."
He. The harvester.
And now here it was.
Juno sat very still for a moment longer.
Then she got up, and pulled on her stockings, and laced her boots, both of them, properly, tight, the way Doctor Silas said, so her feet would not slide. And put on her cap. And wound her scarf round her neck. And put the packet inside her coat, against her chest, on the left side, where the letter had been, all those miles.
Behind the curtain, her mother stirred.
"Juno?" A sleepy, hoarse voice. "Is it morning? Where are you going, love?"
"Saint Bride's," said Juno. "Go back to sleep, Ma. I'll be back by dark."
"Mind your feet."
"I will."
And she went out through the purple door and up the passage that smelled of coal and cats, and out into the gray street, and began to run.
